it in the air and could catch it but it would appear that there has been at
least no attempt on the part of the Japanese to interfere with this service
as it would be a very simple matter for the Japanese to fly a pursuit ship
to a high altitude in the neighborhood of Hongkong and wait for the Burasia
plane to leave Hongkong on its daily schedule and then catch the Eurasia
plane over Chinese territory.
As I say this would be a very simple matter
because the Eurasia plane arrives and leaves on a published schedule.
The other route proposed to be flown would be from Chungking
to Kweilin to Hongkong and the Managing Director claims that this route
has been approved by the Ministry of Communications.
It would be a DC-2
operation and the only hazzard in my opinion would be that now run by
Eurasia in its operations round about Hongkong.
The merit in the plan as outlined in my hastily written per-
sonal letter to you dispatched by the last flight and the radio 143, is
that a method is provided by which we can protect PAA's investment which

Letter No. B-23-37.
Pan American Airways Company
New York.
Attention Mr. Morgan:
P A N
Dear Mr. Morgan:
I was very much interested in your letter of September 22nd and
your analysis of the developments which led up to the opening of the Sino.
Japanese hostilities would seem to indicate that a student of Chinese af-
fairs far removed from the daily gossip and rumors of the street is probab-
ly in a better position to judge the value of the forces than one who is,
as you state, so close to the trees that he can't see the woods.
I do not entirely agree with you that China
"came out from under the desk
with a brass knuckle on either hand".
It is true that China has been pre-
paring but that preparation was no where near complete as evidenced by
fact that China ia already running short of many essential materials.
go on to say that there is considerable talk in New York and elsewhere to
the effect that the Chinese Government was dragged into the war through
publie opinion and inability to restrain the military leaders and masses
of the people any longer and then you go on to state that in your opinion
this theory is unsound and point in support of your position to the ample
preparations made against a war with Japan.
I am personally still of the opinion that Chiang Kai-shek wes
and desired to go to any ends rather than permit the starting
of hostilities which might lead to his own overthrow and a complete de•
feat of China.
I believe he would have gladly worked out some compromise
for & show of war in the North to be followed by definite concessions in-
cluding an autonomous state in the Province of Hopei and probably north
Shantung•
Most authorities agree that the actual starting of hostilities
in the Shanghai area was brought on by the Chinese rather than the Japanese
as the latter had been unusually conciliatory with respect to all incidents
in the Shanghai area.
In this connection I had a very interesting talk
with a man here who is known to you as an outstanding military strategist.
He states that only the results justify the action of the Japanese in de-
fending
their position at Shanghai. It was known that there were only
10,000 Japanese troops in the Shanghai area as against not less than 60,000
Chinese,
including the best troops that General Chiang could put in the
field.
I told this party that a Chinese official informed me on the night
of August 14th that the Japanese would be pushed into the Whangpoo that
night and the same party repeated that statement on the 15th.
Our mutual
friend here stated that there wes no excuse whatever for the Chinese not
completing that objective and that if he had been in the position of the
Japanese Commander he would have taken to the boats and left Shanghai
-1 3 !

immediately.
It seems to me that some of the hot headed military men under
General Chiang forced his hand in expectation of destroying all Japanese
boats in the Whangpoo and wiping out the small Japanese garrison. The
Chinese no doubt placed a great deal more confidence in their Air Force
then subsequent events have justified.
It is true of course that the Chines e
Air Force should have blown every Japanese boat out of the Whengpoo during
the first two or three days of the conflict and should also have prevented
the landing of troops at Woosung or for that matter even the approach of
airplane carriers or transports.
So far as your comment upon the Japanese action at Shanghai is
concerned in spite of what you say to the contrary,
there was no real need
for the Japanese to take Shanghai as it would have been very simple for the
Japanese to have stopped all ships at the entrance to the Yangtsze and thus
have blocked Shanghai as effectively as they have blocked Canton or Tsingtag
for instance, at neither of which places have they landed any troops.
I note your opinion that the wer will be long drawn out provided
China can get the necessary supplies.
It is true as you point out that there
is no gasoline produced in China but large quantities have been shipped in
through Hongkong and when this source of supply is eliminated through des-
truction of the Canton Kowloon Railroad then the Chinese will have to rely
for a gasoline supply on the highway from Russia running to Urumohi, Hami
and Lanchow and on the overland routes from Yunnenfu, which place is in turn
served as you know by the railroad to Hanoi.
It is extremely unlikely in
my opinion that the Japanese will be able to put that railroad out of com-
mission as it is too far removed from any base the Japanese are likely to
estanlish on the south China cosst.
I was particularly impressed by the analysis contained in the
first paragraph on the last page of your letter. I quite agree with you
that the Chinese have only one chance of winning, namely, by bleeding the
Japanese eonomically and financially white and that is obviously their in-
I now come to that part of your letter which bears on the pres-
ent situation particularly in view of my long cable No. 143. I note that yo u
say that in your"opinion there is not the slightest chance of our resuming op-
erations or participating in operations in China even if we were disposed to
make the necessary further investment.
In light of what has happened I be-
lieve that it will be possible to operate provided we divide our operations
into two distinot sections as indicated in my wire under reference.
I believe
we should base the DC-2's at either
Chungking or Chengtu as in my opinion
neither of those cities will be bombed by the Japanese except as a stunt.
You must remember that the distance from Shanghai to Chunking is 1000 miles
and that a Japanese bomber operating from Shanghai or for that matter any
point now held by the Japanese in North China, would have to fly 2000 miles
in order to bomb Chungking•
As I say, this could possibly be done as a
stunt but the fact that the Japanese have not as yet*bombed Hankow which is
only 450 miles airline from Shanghai would indicate thet they do not have
any bombers capable of flying say 1000 miles with a load of bombs.
Certain-
ly if they could have bombed Hankow they would have done so for it is en im-
portant reilroad center.
Therefore if we base at Chungking it should be
quite safe. Operation by Douglas from Chungking to Ichang should be quite

Letter No. B-23-37
Morgan
A discussion of operations necessarily involves available personnel.
In this connection I should say that CNAC has three Chinese pilots who have
proved their ability on seaplanes. There are two other pilots who could be
quickly checked out on Commodores and I am sure do a very creditable job as
the two pilots in question are the senior Chinese pilots but one in the ser-
vice of the Company.
The No. 1 Chinese pilot, Donald Wong, was so abused
by the Chinese management that he finally deserted and has returned to the
For American pilots we
• have Sweet
and Harry Smith, both of
whom have been flying the DC-2's and are old experienced airline pilots.
would have to add one more American pilot and would probably offer the position
to either Sharp or Woods who are now in Java on vacation.
Both of these pilots
have accepted positions with Panagra but we could withhold one of them if he
were willing to accept an assignment with CNAC.
The Chinese communications
organization is intact as is also the motor mechanics overhaul and all ground
personnel fornerly stationed at Lunghwa. Oscar Wilke, Chief Mechanic, is
standing by watohing developments and if any such plan as that outlined in
cable 143 is worked out he will be willing to again join CNAC.
Larsen, one
of our oldest and best mechanics is now with CNAC and another American
anie Haynie, is aleo with the present Company.
With this nucleus of Amer-
ican mechanics it would be entirely practicable to give the air planes and
motors proper service and maintenance.
Mr. Bond is willing to serve as
Operations Manager and believes that with this organization he would be able
to make a creditable showing.
Eurasia is operating at a profit for the first time in its ex-
faot that surface transportation is practically at a stand -
still. However it is only a question of time in my opinion before Eurasia
will have to abandon its base at Hankow and probably also the Sian base and
when that time comes passengers now oa ried from Hankow to Hongkong by Eurasia
would have to travel on the proposed CNAC line from Chungking to Hongkong; also
all international mail and a majority of domestic airmail would travel over
The present Managing Director, Lum Wei-shing is apparently desir-
ous only of bringing the Americans back into the operations of CNAC and then
he will be willing I believe to withdraw and join the Aviation Commission.
When I saw him in Hongkong he very carefully avoided any criticism whatever
of the American interest, dissembled a great friendship for me although I know
that none exists, made no mention of our holding the DC-2 at Hongkong and in
fact on his return to Hankow made good his promise and delivered a check to
Mr. Bond for $100,000 as he had promised he would do.
With Lum Wei-shing out
the picture and P. Y. Wong in as Managing Director we should be able to
get along much better than we ever have at any time in the past.
To sum up the whole situation the vantages of re-association are
(1) Immediate recognition by the Chinese Government of the value of the Amer-
ican shares in CNAC as of July 3lst.
(2) Extension of the contract.
Purchase of Route 3 (I suggested $300,000 U.S. in order to have a fixed sum
which would at once be recognized as materially below our actual into tre
at the same time represent an amount which I think we can get.)
Provide for immediate payment of the balance of CNAC's account as well as
purchase of the Dolphin and the purchase of the two Commodores.

As against the advantages of this program there is nothing to lod
forward to other than a very dubious claim against a reluctant and contentiaus
creditor, the Chinese Government, when the war is over.
recent statements of President Roosevelt and the State Department
have created a very favorable sentiment towards the United States.
Also the
Chinese Aviation Commission which was so arrogant and self sufficient has made
a miserable failure and proven conclusively that the Chinese Air Force without
American or other foreign assistance is a hopeless failure.
In CNAC this same
situation has developed and our Chinese associates realize that unless American
supervision of mechanical work and flight routine is reestablished that CNAC
will have nothing left in another thirty days.
It is clear that the opinions
of men like I. V. Soong who have always maintained that the Chinese are not yet
ready to take over their own aviation activities, are now prevailing and there
is an insistent demand on the Ministry that negotiations be undertaken to assure
the return of American cooperation and technical assistance.
T. V. Soong knows
for instance that we were forced out by a series of high handed
and silly orders
issued by the Ministry of Communications and there is no doubt in my mind but
that he and men like him have had a showdown and have issued an ultimatum to
Lum Wei-shing and the Ministry demanding that such steps be taken as necessary
within reason to bring us back into the picture.
In our conference at Hongkong on October 6th Mr. Bond and P. Y. Wong
said that the Managing Director talked of nothing
else but persuading me to ro-
turn with him to Nanking.
When I suggested to P. Y. Wong that Mr. Bond could
do everything that I could hope to accomp11sh at Nanking, PI. Wont sceply
was that they wanted the No. 1 which I am sure is only a matter of
the M. Do as he must be extremely antagonistic to me because of the withdrawal
American interest and the holding of the D. CIwo at Hongkong. In short
I know that the M. D. would much prefer to deal with Mr. Bond and his only
reason for wanting me back is that he must have been told to do whatever neces-
sary to close the breach that existed between us.
I am perfectly willing to go to Nanking provided you give me auth-
ority to make the best deal I can make in the interests of the Company.
would of course wish to establish a minimum which you are prepared to accept
and I would attempt to get as much above that minimum as possible. However
it will be impossible to clear details from Nanking as comunications from
there are extremely diffioult.
I would expeot to either close a satisfactory
deal or leave Nanking within a period of one week and would announce such in-
tention at the opening of negotiations.
Very truly yours,
PAN AMERICAN AIRWAYS
COMPANY
